1762: The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute which led to the merger of the former State into the Matsya Union. He applied for and was granted a permit for export of 15,000 maunds of chuni with which he deposited Rs. 30,000/as export duty in advance. His case further was that though he asked the State for refund of this advance duty, the State did not pay back the same to him. In reply to this contention the respondent relied on article 295(2) of the Constitution and other provisions made during the period when mergers were taking place after August 15, 1947 and contended that in view of article 295 (2) of his case the new State of Dholpur was bound by the obligation of the former Part B State of Rajasthan to meet the liabilities of all old States which ultimately were included in it subject always to this that if the new State passed any law repealing the old laws then the new State would be liable under article 295 of the Constitution. Held: (i) Article 295(1) of the Covenant is an independent provision of the Constitution which has been enacted by the President and the Governor General in Council and the President cannot override the Constitutional limitations imposed upon the State by the Covenant or by the Constitution. The guarantee contained in article 295 is only for the purpose of securing the continuance of existing laws and does not confer any additional rights on the citizens. The guarantee of equality before the law and equal protection of the laws is a sine qua non for the existence of the rule of law and the enforcement of the guarantee cannot be denied. It is only where there is no violation of the fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution that the Court can refuse relief. The guarantee under article 296(2) is not merely of a kind as to the person who is to bear the liability but also of a character different from what is guaranteed in the Constitution. It is not a mere guarantee of the right to move the court for the enforcement of such a right; it is a guarantee against arbitrary action by the executive authorities. The guarantee given under article 297(2) must therefore be confined to matters of public concern and should not extend beyond the limits provided by the Constitution
